Enhancing Anaerobic Digestion of Food Waste by Combining
Carriers and Microaeration: Performance and Potential Mechanisms
Published as part of ACS ES&T Engineering special issue“ Low-Carbon Resource Utilization and Pollution
Control of Solid Wastes ”.

ABSTRACT: Enhancing the anaerobic digestion (AD) of organic
wastes has been a widely discussed topic. This study aims to enhance
AD performance by combining microaeration with conductive or
nonconductive carriers, using food waste as the substrate. The use of
carriers alone enhanced methane production, and microaeration
further improved performance. The conductive carrier showed
significant enhancement with microaeration, achieving a daily
methane yield of 478 ± 11.3 mL CH4/g VS, which was 1.1 and
1.3 times higher than that of the nonconductive carrier and the
control digester, respectively. Furthermore, the study explored
various aspects, including oxidative stress, antioxidant capacity, and
microbial community structure during digestion. The results
demonstrated that combining microaeration with a conductive
carrier improved hydrolytic-acidification efficiency and promoted direct interspecies electron transfer among syntrophic
microorganisms. Methanogenic archaea aggregated on the carrier surface and formed consortia with facultative anaerobes, thereby
mitigating oxidative stress effects on cells and enhancing total methane production. Moreover, metabolomics analysis showed that
combining conductive carriers with microaeration enhanced ATP transport across the bacterial membrane, accelerated nutrient
conversion, and caused significant changes in metabolites and intermediates related to glycerophospholipids, amino acids, and signal
transduction pathways.
KEYWORDS: anaerobic digestion, microaeration, carrier, oxidative stress, metabonomics
1. INTRODUCTION
In recent years, the management of municipal solid waste
(MSW) has become a significant global environmental
challenge. In 2019, over 2 billion tonnes of MSW were
produced globally, with projections suggesting a potential 70%
increase by 2050.1 The China Statistical Yearbook (2020)
reported that MSW production in China has steadily risen at a
rate of 5−6% annually, reaching 254.79 million tons in 2020,
while food waste (FW) production in China ranged between
72.44 million to 127.40 million tons, comprising 30−50% of all
MSW in the same year.2 FW contains valuable carbohydrates,
proteins, lipids, and minerals, making it an ideal raw material
for biofuel production via microbial conversion.3 Anaerobic
digestion (AD) is a key process in the microbial conversion of
FW. During digestion, fermenting bacteria and methanogenic
archaea work together to convert organic compounds in FW
into methane and carbon dioxide. This process involves stages
such as hydrolysis, acidification, hydrogen-producing aceto-
genesis, and methanogenesis. Methane, as a clean fuel, has
significant applications in the energy supply and industrial
production. Therefore, enhancing the efficiency of converting
FW organics to methane is critical. Various methods have been
employed to enhance the hydrolytic-acidification efficiency,
including pretreatments (e.g., mechanical, thermal, and acid/
alkali),4 microaeration,5,6 and the use of exogenous additives.7,8
Microaeration involves injecting small amounts of air or
oxygen (typically ranging from 0.005 to 5 L O2/L reactor/day)
into an anaerobic system, and it has garnered considerable
research attention for its potential to improve the hydrolytic-
acidification process in the digestion of various organic
substrates.9−11 Injecting small amounts of air creates a higher

oxidation−reduction potential (ORP) environment compared
with strict anaerobic conditions, thereby reshaping the
microbial community in the digester. Facultative anaerobes
involved in the hydrolytic-acidification process exhibit higher
activities under these conditions. Fu et al.5 demonstrated that
introducing microaeration at an air load of 12.5 mL/LR per day
in the AD of corn stover enhanced the biodiversity of
facultative hydrolytic and acidifying bacteria. Furthermore,
according to Yu et al.,12 appropriate microaeration (5 mg O2/
L-reactor/cycle) not only enhanced the hydrolytic-acidification
process in the digestion of black water but also improved the
methanogenesis efficiency. The ORP variation induced by
microaeration also had domestication effects on the archaeal
community. Higher abundance of hydrogenotrophic metha-
nogens with stronger toxic tolerant ability was commonly
observed in the microaerated digesters.
In addition, the syntrophic interaction between bacteria and
methanogenic archaea is another crucial factor determining the
AD efficiency.13 These microorganisms have unique yet
complementary metabolic capabilities, exchanging electrons
via H2 as electron shuttles for energy. Establishing direct
interspecies electron transfer (DIET) between bacteria and
archaea is essential for efficient electron communication. DIET
established by exogenous conductive materials enhances both
the transfer rate and efficiency by building an electron bridge
between syntrophic oxidation bacteria and methanogens while
also avoiding mass-transfer resistance through interspecies
hydrogen transfer. Thus, the combination of microaeration and
conductive materials holds promise for achieving significant
improvements. Our previous research has shown that
combining CaO2 (0.01 g/L) and magnetite (0.4 g/L)
synergistically enhanced the conversion of organic matter,
optimizing the relationship between fermentative bacteria and
methanogenic archaea to increase methane production over-
all.14 The release of O2 or H2O2 during CaO2 decomposition
can be considered another form of microaeration. Additionally,
microaeration introduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) into
the reactor, resulting in their accumulation, inducing toxic
oxidative stress in cells or organisms. This stress can lead to
oxidative damage to microbial activity (or central metabolism)
and important cellular molecules (e.g., DNA damage and
protein inactivation).15,16 Therefore, given the toxicity of these
oxidative agents to anaerobic microbes, precise control of
oxygen dosage is crucial to prevent oxidative stress on strict
anaerobic functional communities, especially oxygen intolerant
methanogenic archaea. Furthermore, the substantial biomass
loss during feeding and discharging exacerbated challenges for
anaerobic microorganisms coping with oxidative stress,
particularly slow growing methanogens that could be easily
screened out during sludge discharge, leading to system failures
in long-term microaeration applications.
Introducing carriers like zeolite,17 nonwoven fabric18 and
fibers19 into the digestive system can effectively retain slow
growing anaerobic microorganisms, reducing excessive loss of
functional microorganisms during semicontinuous AD oper-
ation with daily feeding and discharging. Carriers with
conductive properties were preferred because they not only
induced anaerobic biofilm formation but also promoted the
DIET mechanism. Liu et al.19 discovered that gaps and pores
in fibrous carriers facilitated anaerobe attachment during corn
straw AD, enabling easy contact between microorganisms and
the substrate. Zhuravleva et al.20 observed that biofilms were
more abundant on carbon cloth than on fiberglass cloth in a
continuous flow bioreactor, and using carbon cloth improved
DIET between electrogenic and electrotrophic microorgan-
isms. Microbial biofilms consist of cells embedded in a three-
dimensional extracellular matrix that acts as a scaffold for cell
adhesion, supports mature biofilm structure formation, and
protects cells from harsh environmental conditions.21−23 From
the aspect of oxygen toleration for microbes, the formation of
biofilm on the carrier’s surface may present a certain protection
on strict anaerobes.15
Based upon analysis, microaeration has been shown to
enhance the hydrolytic-acidification process. Additionally,
conductive carriers may facilitate efficient electron communi-
cation between archaea and bacteria while protecting strict
anaerobes from oxidative stress. Therefore, combining
microaeration and conductive carriers in an AD system is
expected to greatly improve the digestive performance. No
relevant reports have been found to date. Thus, this study
aimed to regulate the digestive system in semicontinuous AD
of FW by combining microaeration and conductive carriers.
Specifically, our objectives were: (1) to improve hydrolytic-
acidification efficiency to supply adequate substrates for
methanogenic archaea and (2) to establish effective electron
communication and metabolic balance between bacteria and
archaea to ensure efficient utilization of bacterial metabolic
products and maintain system stability. To achieve these
objectives, the study initially analyzed digestive performance to
assess the promotional effect. Cell viability analysis, enzyme
activity measurement, and microbial community analysis were
used to understand microbial metabolic activities under such
artificial conditions. Furthermore, metabolomics analysis was
employed to elucidate the internal mechanisms of micro-
organisms. The results of this study may provide new insights
and references for further improving the AD efficiency.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Substrates and Inoculum. The anaerobic inoculum
was sourced from a wastewater treatment plant in Chongqing,
China. The substrate FW was prepared in the laboratory
according to the formula described by Li et al.24 Characteristics
of both the substrate and inoculum are detailed in Table S1.
2.2. Digester Setup and Operational Conditions. The
AD system comprises a feed hopper, a mixing shaft, a separate
jacketed thermostat, and a gas collection device. Each reactor
was constructed from a plexiglass cylinder (inner diameter 8
cm, height 25 cm) with a working volume of 0.7 L and a
headspace of 0.3 L. The carrier filling ratio in this study was
20%, determined as optimal from preliminary experiments
(Figure S1). The experimental group with added carriers
included two reactors: one containing carbonaceous honey-
comb-like carrier (noted as T20) (2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm,
Suzhou Carbon whirlwind Carbon Co. Ltd., China) and the
other packed with polyurethane sponge without conductivity
(noted as D20) (2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm, Henan Tianyi
Environmental Protection Science and Technology Co. Ltd.,
China). Detailed characteristics of the carriers can be found in
Table S2. The digester without a carrier served as the control
group (noted as D0). The AD systems operated in the
semicontinuous feeding mode to maintain a constant hydraulic
retention time of 20 d, with an organic loading rate of 2.5 g
VS/L·d and a digestion temperature of 35 ± 1 °C. The entire
experimental process comprised three stages: initiation (stage
I), nonaeration (stage II), and microaeration (stage III). In the
third stage, air was injected into the digesters at a dose of 5 mL

were carried out in triplicate.
2.3. Chemical and Physical Analysis. Measurements of
total solid (TS), volatile solid (VS), chemical oxygen demand,
and NH4
+-N were conducted in accordance with standard
methods.25 pH was determined by a pH meter (FE28,
METTLER TOLEDO, Switzerland). Conductivity was meas-
ured by a conductivity meter (DDS-11A/307, Yueping,
Shanghai). The biogas composition and volatile fatty acids
(VFAs) were determined by gas chromatography (GC1690,
Jiedao, Hangzhou). The operation process of gas chromatog-
raphy was introduced in detail in previous study.26 The
extraction method of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS)
referred to the study of Li et al.27 Based on the difficulty of
component and bacterial separation as well as spatial
distribution, EPS was subdivided into three layers: soluble
EPS (SEPS), loosely bound EPS (LB-EPS), and tightly bound
EPS (TB-EPS). The PN and PS of each form of EPS were
determined as the total amount by the Lowry−Folin method
and phenol-sulfuric acid method, respectively.28 According to
Limbach et al.,29 the intracellular ROS production was
determined using 2′7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate
(H2DCFDA; Molecular Probes, Eugene, USA). Electron
transfer activity (ETS) was measured using the method
reported by Luo et al.30 α-Glucosidase activity, ATP content,
catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), superoxide
reductase (SOR), nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+/
NADH), as well as acetate kinase (ACK) were measured by
using the ELISA kit (Shanghai hengyuan biological technology
co., LTD).
2.4. Microbiological Analysis. Anaerobic biofilms on the
surface of the carrier and digested sludge were detected by
scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800, Leica,
Germany). The presence of a carrier may create a physical
barrier or provide an attachment point, thereby impeding or
enhancing the contact of the colorant with the micro-
organisms. Therefore, in this study, sludge samples were
collected for staining to assess the effectiveness of carriers in
enhancing cell viability and optimizing microbial activity
during AD after the introduction of microaeration. The cell
viability of the sludge samples was stained using Live/Dead
BacLight bacterial viability staining kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad,
CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and
observation using a confocal laser scanning microscope (ZEISS
Axio Scan, Z1, Germany). Fluorescence in situ hybridization
(FISH) analysis was performed on biomass samples fixed with
4% paraformaldehyde solution.31 This study utilized oligonu-
cleotide probes specific for bacteria (FITC-labeled EU-
B338mix probes) and archaea (Cy3-labeled ARC915 probe).
The labeled samples were visualized using an Olympus BX41
epifluorescence microscope (Olympus, USA) (Table S3). At
the end of each stage, samples were taken from the digester for
microbial community structure analysis. To explore the
differences in bacterial metabolic characteristics, six biomass
samples were collected from each reactor for metabolite
analysis at the end of the experiment to ensure the reliability of
the experimental results. The details of the analytical methods
used above are available in the Supporting Information.
2.5. Statistical Analysis. The experimental data under-
went analysis of variance (ANOVA) for statistical processing.
All physicochemical index data presented in this paper are
expressed as “mean ± standard deviation” (n = 3) to enhance
clarity. Student’s t-test was used to assess significant differences
between different systems, with a p-value below 0.05
considered statistically significant. Statistical mapping was
performed by using Origin 9.0 software.
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Anaerobic Digestion Performance. The digestion
performance of various digesters is depicted in Figure 1.
Methanogenic properties are commonly believed to directly
reflect the adaptability of the anaerobic microbiome in AD.32
Figure 1 shows that methane production achieved stable after
an short time start and varies among different digesters.
Clearly, the application with carrier materials significantly
enhanced methane production (p < 0.05). The averaged
methane yield for the control digester was approximately 329
± 19.1 mL CH4/g VS, whereas for the D20 and T20 in this
stage were 394 ± 12.5 and 420 ± 17.9 mL CH4/g VS,
respectively. These results indicated that carrier materials
positively enhanced digestion performance, especially con-
ductive carriers, which exhibited a greater promotional effect
compared to nonconductive ones.33
Trace amount of air was added at the end of stage II (30
days). In this stage (stage III), it can be noted that the
application of microaeration gives a further promotion of the
methane production. For the control digester, the methane
production was increased from 329 ± 19.1 mL CH4/g VS at

VFAs, such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are
important intermediate products in the AD process. Accumu-
lation of VFAs in the digester can lower the pH and inhibit
methane production. Following the introduction of microaera-
tion (stage III), D0 exhibited significant fluctuations in specific
methane yield and TVFA levels, with a noticeable trend toward
accumulation over time (Figure 1b). A rapid increase in TVFA
concentration was observed in this digester after 35 days of
digestion following the introduction of microaeration,
accompanied by decreased methane production and pH,
suggesting system acidification. This result verified our
assertion in the introduction that the application of
microaeration needs to be well controlled to avoid its potential
damage to obligate anaerobes. However, when the microaera-
tion is combined with carriers, the system stability was much
more enhanced. Despite inevitable fluctuations in VFA
concentrations, they consistently remained below 300 mg/L
throughout the experimental period. Furthermore, the VFA
concentration of the T20 was much lower than that in the
D20, possibly due to enhanced VFA consumption facilitated
by the conductive material.34 Overall, combining carriers with
microaeration mitigates its adverse effects on obligate anae-
robes, especially for some methanogens, which is helpful to
maintain the system stability. Moreover, the combined use of
conductive carrier and microaeration demonstrated a more
favorable effect.
3.2. Oxidative Stress and Antioxidant Ability.
Exposure of microorganisms to oxygen leads to the
accumulation of molecular oxygen within the cell, resulting
in the production of large quantities of ROS (i.e., O2
•−, H2O2,
and
•OH), which can cause oxidative stress, enzyme
inactivation, and interference with microbial morphology and
structural integrity.35 Figure 2 showed the ROS intensities in
different digesters, indicating that the use of carrier materials
improves the ROS intensity. The ROS intensity in D20 with
the nonconductive polyurethane sponge was 117% higher than
the control digester with microaeration solely. Conductive
carriers promoted ROS intensity even further, with an increase
of 157% compared to the control. The reason for this is that
polymer synthetic hydrophilic biological carrier, characterized
by interconnected pores that increase contact area and time,
allows oxygen to remain within the carrier. This promoted
interactions between oxygen and microbial cells, while also
modifying pH, temperature, and nutrient supply to create
favorable conditions for ROS production.36,37 The conductive
carrier materials could promote electrochemical reactions
within the digester,38 leading to increased electron-transfer
processes and further promoting the generation of ROS
through mechanisms such as electron capture by oxygen.
Notably, the higher quantity of microbes in the conductive
material group may promote microbial proliferation and
metabolic activity, thereby contributing to the elevated ROS
levels in T20 (Figure 5). Additionally, conductive carriers were
optimal catalysts for H2O2 production due to their high
selectivity for the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction, good
electrical conductivity, and nontoxicity.39 ROS can serve as
terminal electron receptors for anaerobic respiration and
support the proliferation of facultative anaerobic bacteria,
contributing to enhance hydrolytic-acidification processes and
accelerate the conversion of particulate organic matter to
dissolved ones.40 In addition, ROS also has strong oxidizing
ability, which can produce free radicals and help oxidize
various refractory organics.41,42
Prolonged exposure of cells to ROS can induce cellular
damage. In response, microorganisms can produce antiox-
idative enzymes like CAT, SOR, and SOD to neutralize
harmful oxidants, converting them into harmless products and
preventing damage to cellular components.43 Specifically, SOD
and SOR primarily mitigate damage caused by O2
•−in
anaerobic systems by reducing O2
•−peroxyl radicals to H2O2.
CAT catalyzes the decomposition of H2O2 into O2 and H2O,
thereby reducing its potentially toxic effects on anaerobic
microorganisms. As depicted in Figure 2a, following prolonged
exposure to microaeration, the levels of SOD, SOR, and CAT
in D20 were 104.8, 148.5, and 116.9%, respectively, compared
to those in D0. Furthermore, in T20 exposed to microaeration,
the levels of SOD, SOR, and CAT were further increased to
107.7, 201.4, and 136.1% of the control, indicating that
conductive carrier enhanced the antioxidant capacity of the
digester. Enhanced production of antioxidant enzymes helped
microorganisms mitigate the adverse effects of excessive ROS

EPS, a polymer secreted by microorganisms in specific
environments, envelops nearly all microbial cells, crucially
facilitating biofilm formation, maintaining sludge agglomerate
structure, and shielding microbial cells from adverse environ-
mental conditions.45−47 It was presumed that it may contribute
to microbial aggregate formation and protect microorganisms
from oxygen stress. Thus, EPS levels were quantified in the
sludge following stable operation of each group (Figure 2b).
Data revealed that SEPS predominated in the control group,
whereas TB-EPS constituted the majority in carrier-containing
sludge samples. SEPS were weakly bound with cells or
absolutely dissolved into bulk solution,48 suggesting that
long-term microaeration could disrupt the original stable
sludge structure, promote the conversion of other EPS forms
into SEPS, and increase the possibility of sludge loss. This
finding also elucidated why the carrier group exhibited superior
operational effectiveness compared to that of the control
group. TB-EPS plays an indispensable role in promoting sludge
agglomeration and granulation by condensing cells and inert
particles together through a solid physicochemical connection,
resulting in a more compact and compacted sludge structure.49
The contents of TB-EPS in the control group, D20, and T20
groups were 216.0, 586.3, and 689.5 mg/L, respectively.
Furthermore, protein, an important component of EPS, had
the highest content in T20, suggesting that microorganisms
were stimulated by microaeration and enhanced the secretion
of proteins (Table S4), which further promoted the content of
TB-EPS and strengthened the adhesion of cells to each other,
finally forming microbial aggregates. Microbial aggregates
shield organisms living deep inside diffusion barriers,
preventing the full penetration by oxygen.50
3.3. Enzymes and ETS Activities. AD is catalyzed by
microorganisms, including hydrolytic acidification bacteria and
methanogenic archaea, and involves synergistic actions of
various enzymes. To assess how microaeration and carriers
influence microbial activities, the activities of relevant enzymes
and the ETS were analyzed (Figure 3). In stage II without
microaeration, the presence of carriers elevated the activities of
the relevant enzymes, indicating enhanced colonization of
microorganisms and biofilm formation, leading to greater
metabolic activity. Moreover, the inherent conductivity of the
conductive carrier facilitated electron transfer, further enhanc-
ing enzyme activity and ETS. With microaeration introduction,
enzyme activity and ETS further increased, indicating
enhanced microbial activity. Subsequent discussion will focus
on microaeration’s promotion of enzyme activities.
α-glucosidase plays an important role in the hydrolysis of
polysaccharides, facilitating the conversion of complex organic
solids into soluble small molecules for microbial utilization.51
The activity of α-glucosidase significantly increased after
microaeration (p < 0.05), with the control group showing an
increase from 266 IU/L to approximately 341 IU/L. Digesters
with carriers showed greater improvements, reaching 401 IU/L
(D20) and 494 IU/L (T20), which were 118% and 159%
higher than those in the control digester. Similarly,
microaeration resulted in an increase in the activity of ACK,
particularly in digesters with conductive carriers (184 to 202
U/L). These heightened activities of α-glucosidase and ACK
provide evidence of the improvements brought about by
microaeration and its synergistic combination with conductive
carriers. Ruan et al.51 observed that microaeration can
effectively stimulate the activities of hydrolytic enzymes of
facultative bacteria and enhance the activity of AD micro-
organisms. Furthermore, microaeration provided exogenous
electron acceptors that facilitated the adjustment of bacteria
from the reduction process with H+ as the electron acceptor to
the respiratory process with trace electron acceptors such as
O2, resulting in higher levels of energy metabolism.14,52
ATP, as the direct source of energy in living organisms,
reflects cellular energy status and plays a critical role in
regulating cellular metabolism.53 During stage III, ATP activity
exhibited a significant increase, with D20 and T20 digesters
showing approximately 120% and 126% higher ATP activities
compared to the control group. This increase in ATP activity
may be attributed to microaeration stimulating the trans-
membrane transport of protons (significant enrichment of
ABC transporter proteins) (Figure 7), thereby enhancing ATP
synthesis. Moreover, as more acetyl-CoA flows into the
tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to produce ATP, more
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) is produced.54
Reduction of O2 with NADH releases a significant amount of
energy, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis
and the transport of other metabolites.9

NAD (H/+) is a crucial cofactor in various biochemical
processes within the cell.55 NADH provides the necessary
reduction equivalent for intracellular reduction, while NAD+
serves as an electron acceptor in intracellular NAD+ dependent
oxidation reactions. Monitoring the NADH/NAD+ ratio is
critical in assessing the fermentation efficiency during the
digestion process.56 The addition of microaeration resulted in
a slight increase in NAD+ activity in T20, reaching 89.4 U/L,
which was 154% and 111% higher than D0 and D20,
respectively. Conversely, NADH activity significantly increased
from 119.2 to 144.1 U/L, resulting in an approximately 15%
higher ratio of NADH/NAD+ ratio to 1.6. The lack of electron
acceptors (e.g., oxygen) during the second stage may have
inhibited the electron-transfer process and NAD+ produc-
tion.57 Introducing microaeration stimulated the TCA cycle
and enhanced NADH production. Furthermore, the increased
activity of hydrolases after microaeration promoted the
hydrolysis of polysaccharide organic matter, leading to the
consumption of NAD+ during glucose molecule catabolism55
and consequently elevated NADH/NAD+ values. High
NADH/NAD+ ratios positively regulated O2
•−production,58
reducing ROS induced stress.
ETS activity is an effective indicator of microbial and sludge
biological activity. The introduction of microaeration had a
slight impact on ETS activity in the control group but
significantly improved activity in the carriers’ utilized groups.
The ETS activity of digester D20 increased from 138% to
183%, while T20 showed the highest ETS activity and
conductivity, reaching 201% and 115% of the control group.
These increases demonstrate enhanced electron transfer
among different microorganisms.59 In addition, conductive
carriers established favorable electron-transfer pathways for
microorganisms, promoting cellular electron transfer and
metabolic processes in microorganisms by maintaining redox
homeostasis.14,60
3.4. Microbial Analysis. 3.4.1. Visualization of Microbial
Characteristics. To visualize the impact of carriers on the
aggregation of bacterial and archaeal cells, FISH analysis was
conducted on suspended sludge (Figure 4). FISH images
showed a notable overlap between red fluorescence from
archaea and green fluorescence from bacteria in carrier groups,
suggesting their spatial proximity. Semiquantitative analysis of
fluorescence intensity indicated that archaeal fluorescence in
the T20 and D20 groups constituted 93.1% and 80.5% of total
bacterial fluorescence intensity, respectively (Figure S3). In
contrast, the red fluorescence intensity in the control group
was only 48.7% of the green fluorescence, suggesting a lower
percentage of archaea compared with the carrier groups and
even half that of the T20 group. These findings suggested that
microorganisms in carrier-based samples were densely
distributed, forming microbial aggregates, which highlighted
carriers’ role in facilitating microorganism attachment and
protecting functional flora from adverse external conditions.
This finding was also supported by the SEM results (Figure
S4). The SEM analysis also revealed the formation of a distinct
bilayer structure in the T20 system, with globular bacteria
enriched in the outer layer and rod-shaped and filamentous
bacteria concentrated in the inner layer. Similar to the results
of Sekiguchi et al.61 that observed microbial aggregates, which
comprise the methanogens’ dominant core and a bacteria-
dominant surface.
3.4.2. Microbial Community Structure. To provide an
accurate comparison among different digesters at various
stages, qPCR was adopted to understand the absolute
abundance of microorganisms in the suspension and on the
carrier. As shown in Figure 5, the abundance of suspended
microorganisms in the carrier-added group was higher than
that in the control group. During stage II, gene copy numbers
of bacteria and archaea in T20 sludge samples were
approximately 127% and 135% higher than that in D20,

3.5. Metabolomic Analysis. 3.5.1. Discriminating Me-
tabolite Analysis. In order to deeply understand the potential
mechanism, untargeted metabolomics analyses were used for
samples in the microaeration stages of the three reactors. A
total of 6111 mass spectra peaks were detected in 18 samples,
corresponding to 696 metabolites. The principal component
analysis and partial least-squares discriminant analysis (PLS-
DA) revealed significant differences between the different
groups (Figure S6). Based on the VIP and p values of the
model OPLS-DA, the Student’s t-test was applied for
discriminating the samples from D0 and D20, D0 and T20,
and D20 and T20 to identify the differential metabolites,
respectively (setting VIP > 1, p < 0.05, FC > 1, or FC < 1). A
Venn diagram was employed to identify significant differential

uncovering 161 unique metabolites with 88 metabolites
common across all control groups.
3.5.2. Metabolic Pathway Analysis. The diverse metabo-
lites coordinate with each other to perform biological functions
during AD. Analyzing and annotating pathways can provide
insights into their functions. Thus, these key metabolites were
annotated using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and
Genomes (KEGG) database to determine the associated
pathways, further elucidating the mechanisms. The top 25
KEGG pathways with the highest degree of enrichment were
selected from the three comparison groups, indicating that the
metabolic pathways of the digestion samples primarily involved
two main functions: metabolism and environmental informa-
tion processing (Figure 7a). These pathways were mainly
concentrated in carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid
metabolism, energy metabolism, and lipid metabolism with
some involvement in the biosynthesis of other secondary
metabolites, membrane transport, and signal transduction,
among others.
The methanogenic pathways were directly or indirectly
associated with the central metabolic pathways. Fluctuations in
these pathways were influenced by changes in the diverse
metabolites. This study constructed a metabolic network of
differential metabolites based on KEGG database pathways to
comprehensively investigate metabolism (Figure 7b). Summa-
rizing significantly enriched pathways revealed that D0, D20,
and T20 samples primarily featured glycerophospholipid
metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and signal transduction
pathways, focusing subsequent analysis on these pathways.
Microorganisms can produce sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate
through the glycerophospholipid metabolism, which is
converted into 3-phosphoserine to enter the glycine, serine,
and threonine metabolism pathway or converted into
phosphoenolpyruvate to participate in the synthesis and
metabolism of phosphatidylglycerol or amino acid (e.g.,
tyrosine, proline, and lysine). Glycerophospholipid, as the
major lipid part of the cell membranes, has a variety of
biological functions, including cell proliferation, differentiation,
and apoptosis. Phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs), phosphati-
dylcholine (PCs), and lysophosphatidylcholine (LysoPCs) are
all types of glycerophospholipids and their derivatives.
LysoPCs, formed by the partial hydrolysis of PCs, are
considered fatty acid oxidation products and can affect the
lipid content in tissues. Increased oxidative stress may disrupt
lipid metabolism and cell membrane synthesis.75 Choline,
which is a main component of PCs, is essential for cell
membrane phospholipids. Elevated choline levels can lead to
oxidative modification of membrane phospholipids, disrupting
membrane structure and causing component accumulation.76
LysoPCs and choline are involved in choline metabolism and
glycerophospholipid metabolism pathways. In the study,
glycerophospholipid derivatives like LysoPC (20:1(11Z)/
0:0) and LysoPC (15:0/0:0) were found to be reduced in
the T20 group (Supporting Information statement), indicating
a potential regulation of cellular oxidative stress by the
conductive carrier, resulting in decreased LysoPC levels.
Furthermore, levels of PCs and PEs were also reduced in
T20 cells following microaeration treatment. PCs are essential
components of cell membranes, while PEs serve as precursors
to PCs and are involved in cell membrane turnover.
Glycerophospholipid derivatives and choline were down-
regulated in the T20 group compared with the control,
indicating that T20 can resist oxidative stress by attenuating
the oxidation of fatty acids, promoting cytokine secretion, and
accelerating the normal biosynthesis of cell membranes, which
is another reason T20 may be resistant to ROS.
Amino acids are mainly derived from the degradation of
proteins and play an important role in biological activities,
providing energy and substances for many biosynthesis
processes in cells. It is worth mentioning that microaeration
treatment changed the metabolism of several amino acids,
including tyrosine, tryptophan, serine, lysine, and proline. For
example, putrescine, ornithine, 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, and
proline involved in the proline metabolic pathway were
significantly altered in the D0 group compared with the T20
group. The highest levels of intermediates were observed,
indicating that microaeration treatment may interfere with the
formation of intermediate products in D0 (without carrier).
Destructive accumulation or metabolism of intermediate
products may affect the oxidative equilibrium and homeostasis
of energy metabolism.76 In contrast, the levels of relevant
intermediate metabolites were significantly reversed in the
carrier group (D20 and T20), reflecting the beneficial function
of the carrier. In AD, amino acid metabolism can also be
decomposed and utilized by some bacterial groups to produce
energy and a series of intermediate metabolites, thus
facilitating decomposition and conversion of organic matters.
Butanoate can be transformed to acetyl-CoA, which can be
further converted to CH4 to produce ATP.77 Succinate and
(S)-Malate were intermediates in the TCA cycle, which were
significantly reduced in the conductive carrier (T20) group.
TCA cycle was the final terminal pathway for carbohydrates,
lipids, and proteins, and the downregulation of intermediate
products indicates that nutrients are rapidly consumed. The
downregulation of its intermediate metabolites in T20
indicated that conductive carriers may accelerate nutrient

4. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPLICATIONS
The combined microaeration and conductive carrier system
presented stable digestive performance and better tolerance to
ROS. The main reasons for the better performance are as
follows: (1) the conductive carrier promoted the conversion of
O2 to ROS and strengthened the hydrolysis of organic matter.
In other words, higher level of ROS and better hydrolysis; (2)
the conductive carrier led to a good communication and
transfer of electrons between bacteria and archaea, which
ensured metabolic balance, facilitated the DIET process among
microorganisms, made the metabolism of both bacteria and
archaea more active, and accelerated the conversion of organic
matter to methane; (3) microorganisms formed clusters on
biological carrier surfaces, and microaeration boosted the
secretion of EPS of microorganisms, which further promoted
the formation of aggregate structure and provides a sheltered
environment for microorganisms, resulting in better antiox-
idant capacity of microorganisms, especially for strict anae-
robes (Figure 8). Additionally, microaeration stimulated
facultative bacteria growth (e.g., Bacteroidota and Actino-
bacteriota) that rapidly consume O2, creating an anaerobic
niche for methane production. Methanogens such as
Methanosarcina maintained archaeal community stability
through antioxidant enzyme secretion (e.g., SOD and SOR)
and strong oxygen tolerance.
